processing: Shaded before picking; the top 'dentō hon gyokuro' lots are shaded under natural straw screens on frames, hand-picked from bushes left to grow naturally rather than trimmed into hedges, then steamed, rolled and dried.
harvest_season: First flush only, picked in May, later than the sencha harvest because shading slows growth; the traditional lots are picked by hand.
appearance_dry: Very fine, long, deep black-green needles, often slightly longer and more elegant than Uji gyokuro.
appearance_liquor: Pale green with a slight thickness and sheen.
appearance_wet: Soft, dark green, tender leaves that fall apart.
taste_profile: Thick, sweet umami with a cool seaweed depth and a distinctly soft, almost dashi-like body; the traditional lots have a rounder, less sharp profile than most other gyokuro.

brewing.notes: The Yame way is extreme: lots of leaf, barely any water at 40–50 °C, two and a half minutes, then sip a few mouthfuls of thick broth. Raise the temperature on later steeps. Try a cold or ice-drip brew on a hot day, and eat the spent leaves at the end.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest by grade and producer, with the traditionally shaded, hand-picked 'Yame dentō hon gyokuro' as the premium tier and competition lots at the very top; machine-harvested, cloth-shaded Yame gyokuro is the everyday tier. Like other gyokuro it is usually rested after refining and released later in the year, so autumn is when the new tea is at its best, and it is meant to be finished within about a year.
description:
Yame, in the hills of southern Fukuoka, grows the largest share of Japan's gyokuro, and the traditional lots from the villages of Hoshino and Kurogi are widely regarded as the benchmark for the style. The region's attachment to straw shading and hand-picking gives a gyokuro that is thicker, rounder and more dashi-like than most.

The top tier, Yame dentō hon gyokuro, follows rules that are now protected as a geographical indication: the bushes are left to grow naturally rather than trimmed into hedges, they are shaded under natural straw screens on frames before the harvest, and the leaf is picked by hand, one tender shoot at a time. It is then steamed, rolled and dried as gyokuro. The yield from a bush grown this way is tiny, which is reflected in the price. Everyday Yame gyokuro, cloth-shaded and machine-harvested, is still a serious tea and far more affordable. Saemidori, Okumidori, Samidori and Yabukita are the main cultivars.

Brewing it the Yame way means lots of leaf and almost no water: 10 g in a small shiboridashi with 80 ml at 40–50 °C for two and a half minutes, poured out to the last drop and drunk in a few slow sips; the second steep is short and a little hotter, and the later ones warmer still. The cup is thick, sweet and deeply savoury, with a cool seaweed note and a soft, almost oily texture; the traditional lots are notably rounder and less sharp than cloth-shaded ones. Drip it over ice for a summer version, and eat the spent leaves at the end.

Labels give producer, grade and often cultivar; 'dentō hon gyokuro' marks the traditional tier and the competition lots sit above even that. Note that 'Yame-cha' on its own usually means the region's excellent sencha, so check that the bag says gyokuro. Like all gyokuro it is normally rested after refining, so the new harvest is at its best from autumn, and it should be finished within about a year.

Taste it against a Uji gyokuro of similar grade and you will have the two reference points of the style.
sources_note: The GI rules for Yame dentō hon gyokuro (natural straw shading, hand picking, naturally grown bushes, minimum shading period) are summarised without quoting the exact day count.
history:
Tea in Yame traces itself to a local tradition: the usual story says the Zen monk Eirin Shuzui returned from Ming China in 1423 and brought seed to what is now Kurogi, founding Reigan-ji temple with the help of a village headman. That account is about tea in general. Gyokuro came later: in the Meiji era Yame's producers were moving from pan-fired to steamed green tea.

More than 40 percent of Japan's gyokuro is reported to be grown here. In the 2007 national tea judging Yame teas took every place from first to 26th, and Yame has won the production-area prize in the gyokuro class of the national tea competition in a row since 2001.

In December 2015 the traditional method was registered under Japan's geographical-indication system as Yame Dentō Hon Gyokuro, number 5 on the register. The rules ask for naturally grown bushes, shading on frames with rice straw or other natural materials rather than covering the plants directly, and picking by hand. The registration says these methods have been handed down for more than 110 years.
